oe: Correct. Section 2-209(2) enforces NOM clauses, but except as between merchants, such a requirement on a merchant's form must be separately signed by the other party. A signature at the bottom of the form isn't a separate signature.
That's the general rule, but the separate-signature requirement protects non-merchants on merchant forms.
The non-merchant needed to sign the clause itself, not just the form.
That's the common-law rule. Section 2-209(2) makes NOM clauses enforceable.
topic: Wk 2 · Modification, waiver & estoppel — Separate signature for NOM

q: A buyer orally agrees to buy 100 widgets for $400. Before delivery, the parties orally agree to double the order to 200 widgets for $800. Nothing is ever put in writing. The seller delivers 100 widgets and refuses to deliver more. What can the buyer enforce?
o: Only the original $400 deal, because the $800 modification needed a signed record.
The full 200-widget modification, because modifications need no consideration.
Nothing, because once the parties tried to modify, the original contract was discharged.
The full modification, because the original deal was under $500 and so the statute never applies.
oe: Correct. Section 2-209(3) requires that § 2-201 be satisfied if the contract as modified is within its provisions. At $800, it is. The original $400 contract needed no writing and remains enforceable (Problem 3-4(a)). The failed modification might still operate as a waiver.
No consideration is needed, but the statute of frauds still applies through § 2-209(3).
The failed modification doesn't wipe out the enforceable original deal.
The test looks at the contract as modified, not the original.
topic: Wk 2 · Modification, waiver & estoppel — Modification raises the price over $500

q: Variation: The parties instead orally agree to buy and sell 100 widgets for $1,000, with no writing. Later they orally agree to cut the deal to 40 widgets for $400. Is the modified deal enforceable?
o: Yes: the contract as modified is under $500, so it isn't within § 2-201 and needs no record.
No: the original $1,000 contract was unenforceable, so nothing can be built on it.
No: the modification needed a signed record because the original contract exceeded $500.
Yes, but only because modifications reducing a party's obligations are always enforceable.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-209(3), the question is whether the contract as modified is within § 2-201. A $400 deal isn't (Problem 3-4(b)).
The modified deal stands on its own as an enforceable modification or new agreement under $500.
The statute looks at the contract as modified.
There's no such rule; it's enforceable because it falls below the threshold.
topic: Wk 2 · Modification, waiver & estoppel — Modification lowers the price under $500
pre: A buyer orally agrees to buy 100 widgets for $400. Before delivery, the parties orally agree to double the order to 200 widgets for $800. Nothing is ever put in writing. The seller delivers 100 widgets and refuses to deliver more. What can the buyer enforce?

q: A signed record calls for 100 widgets at $1,000. The parties later orally agree to increase the order to 110 widgets at the same total price. The seller delivers 100 and refuses the extra 10. Can the buyer enforce the extra 10?
o: Likely not: the record shows 100, and enforcement can't exceed that quantity.
Yes: the original signed record satisfies the statute of frauds for any later modification.
Yes: because the price didn't change, the modification falls outside the statute.
No: oral modifications of signed contracts are always void.
oe: Correct. The existing record shows 100. Section 2-201 limits enforcement to the quantity in the record, so it is an impediment to enforcing the extra 10 (Problem 3-4(c)).
It satisfies the statute only up to the 100 units it shows.
The contract as modified is still $500 or more, and the quantity term changed.
They aren't always void; the problem here is specifically the quantity limit.
topic: Wk 2 · Modification, waiver & estoppel — Adding quantity to a signed deal

q: A signed record calls for 100 widgets at $1,000. The parties later orally agree to reduce the order to 90 widgets for $900. The buyer then demands all 100. Is the oral reduction enforceable?
o: Courts split, because the modification changes the quantity term itself.
Clearly yes: reductions in quantity never require a writing.
Clearly no: any change to a signed contract requires a new signed record.
Clearly yes, because $900 is less than the original $1,000.
oe: Correct. Problem 3-4(d) contrasts Costco v. World Wide Licensing and Zemco v. Navistar. One side says the signed record still shows a contract for at least 90 and a record isn't insufficient because it misstates a term. The other says the modification changes the quantity, so it needs its own signed record.
No such rule exists, and courts disagree on this exact fact pattern.
Not all changes do (see a changed delivery date); the quantity question is unsettled.
Both amounts exceed $500; the question is whether the original record can support the reduced quantity.
topic: Wk 2 · Modification, waiver & estoppel — Reducing quantity in a signed deal

q: A signed record calls for 100 widgets at $1,000, delivery June 1. The parties orally agree to move delivery to July 1. The contract has no NOM clause. Does the statute of frauds bar enforcing the July 1 date?
o: No: the original record still shows the contract and quantity; the date can be wrong.
Yes: every modification of a contract over $500 requires a new signed record.
Yes: delivery dates are essential terms that the statute of frauds requires in writing.
No, but only because a change in delivery date is a waiver rather than a modification.
oe: Correct. Section 2-201 requires only a record indicating a contract and the quantity; the existing record still evidences the modified contract (Problem 3-4(e)). A NOM clause, if present, would be a separate barrier under § 2-209(2).
Section 2-209(3) asks whether the contract as modified satisfies § 2-201. Here the original record does.
Only quantity is essential. Other terms may be omitted or misstated.
It can be a valid modification; the original record simply satisfies the statute.
topic: Wk 2 · Modification, waiver & estoppel — Changing the delivery date

q: A 12-month contract requires 10,000 widgets delivered to the buyer's premises by the 5th of each month. The April, May, and June deliveries all arrive a few days late, and the buyer accepts each without complaint. In July, the buyer sues for damages for the three late deliveries and insists on on-time delivery going forward. Which statement is most accurate?
o: It may insist on time going forward; past claims depend on timely notice of breach.
The buyer has permanently waived the delivery date, because a course of performance has replaced the express term.
The buyer may recover for all three deliveries, because accepting goods never affects a buyer's remedies.
The buyer can't insist on on-time delivery going forward without the seller's consent, because the conduct modified the contract.
oe: Correct. Repeated acquiescence may create a course of performance relevant to waiver (§ 1-303(f)), and any waiver of an executory term can be retracted by reasonable notice (§ 2-209(5)). But acceptance doesn't waive damages only if the buyer gives notice of breach within a reasonable time (§ 2-607(3)(a)); silence for three months risks being barred (Problem 3-5(B)).
Express terms prevail over course of performance where they conflict, and waivers of executory terms can be retracted.
Acceptance doesn't impair other remedies (§ 2-607(2)), but the buyer must still give timely notice of breach or be barred.
A modification requires mutual assent; mere acquiescence is better analyzed as waiver, which is retractable.
topic: Wk 2 · Modification, waiver & estoppel — Accepting late deliveries

q: Variation: The signed agreement also says: “No modification will be binding unless in writing signed by both parties.” The seller argues the late-delivery pattern changed the contract anyway. What's the best analysis?
o: No modification, but a waiver the buyer may retract going forward; estoppel weakens.
The NOM clause makes the late-delivery pattern irrelevant for all purposes, including waiver.
The NOM clause is unenforceable between merchants, so the conduct modified the contract.
The pattern created an irrevocable waiver because the NOM clause shows the parties considered the issue.
oe: Correct. Section 2-209(2) bars unwritten modifications, including by course of performance (which is subject to § 2-209). Under § 2-209(4) the failed modification can be a waiver, retractable as to future deliveries under § 2-209(5) (Problem 3-5(C)).
Section 2-209(4) expressly allows a failed modification to operate as a waiver.
NOM clauses are enforceable between merchants; the separate-signature rule protects only non-merchants.
Waivers of executory terms are retractable unless retraction would be unjust given a material change of position.
topic: Wk 2 · Modification, waiver & estoppel — NOM clause and waiver
pre: A 12-month contract requires 10,000 widgets delivered to the buyer's premises by the 5th of each month. The April, May, and June deliveries all arrive a few days late, and the buyer accepts each without complaint. In July, the buyer sues for damages for the three late deliveries and insists on on-time delivery going forward. Which statement is most accurate?

q: With a NOM clause in place, a buyer orally agrees to let the seller deliver on Tuesdays instead of Mondays. After the first Tuesday delivery, the buyer sends notice that it will require Monday deliveries again starting in two weeks. The seller had already signed a one-year, non-cancellable trucking contract for Tuesday runs in reliance. What's the best analysis?
o: A waiver, retractable for the future unless unjust given the seller's material reliance.
The buyer may retract at any time, because waivers are never binding without consideration.
The NOM clause makes the oral agreement a nullity, so the seller has always been bound to deliver on Mondays.
The waiver is irrevocable for the rest of the contract because the seller delivered once on a Tuesday.
oe: Correct. Section 2-209(5) allows retraction of a waiver affecting an executory portion by reasonable notification, unless retraction would be unjust in view of a material change of position in reliance on the waiver.
Retraction is barred where it would be unjust in light of material reliance.
A failed modification can operate as a waiver under § 2-209(4).
Waivers of future performance are generally retractable; irrevocability depends on reliance, not one delivery.
topic: Wk 2 · Modification, waiver & estoppel — Retracting a waiver

q: A contract contains an anti-waiver clause: “A waiver of any provision will be effective only if in a writing signed by the waiving party, and only for the specific instance stated.” The buyer accepts several late deliveries without objection. The seller argues the buyer waived the delivery date. Which statement best reflects the law?
o: Many courts enforce them, though some let conduct waive them; estoppel remains possible.
Anti-waiver clauses are void because they conflict with § 2-209(4).
The clause makes estoppel unavailable as a matter of law.
The clause means the buyer can recover for past late deliveries without giving notice of breach.
oe: Correct. Problem 3-5(D): courts divide on whether conduct can waive an anti-waiver clause. Either way, the buyer may require strict performance going forward and must give § 2-607(3)(a) notice to preserve claims for past breaches.
Many courts enforce them; § 2-209(4) doesn't expressly address them.
Estoppel turns on reasonable detrimental reliance; the clause weakens but doesn't eliminate it.
The § 2-607(3)(a) notice requirement still applies to accepted goods.
topic: Wk 2 · Modification, waiver & estoppel — Anti-waiver clauses

q: A seller wants to prevent a buyer from complaining about late deliveries. Which of the following correctly matches a doctrine to its requirement?
o: Estoppel requires reasonable, detrimental reliance.
Waiver requires consideration and binds both past and future performance.
Course of performance can arise from a single accepted delivery.
Modification requires only that one party give up a right, without the other's assent.
oe: Correct. The four bases are: modification (mutual assent; binding past and future), waiver (voluntary relinquishment of a known right; retractable going forward), course of performance (repeated performance with acquiescence; must be consistent with express terms), and estoppel (reasonable detrimental reliance).
Waiver needs no consideration, and a waiver of executory terms can be retracted.
It requires repeated occasions.
Modification requires mutual assent. One-sided relinquishment is waiver.
topic: Wk 2 · Modification, waiver & estoppel — Four bases compared

q: A boat dealer tells a buyer, “This hull is fiberglass over a solid mahogany frame.” The dealer never uses the words “warrant” or “guarantee” and later testifies he never meant to make any warranty. The frame is particleboard. Did the dealer make an express warranty?
o: Yes: a factual affirmation in the bargain is a warranty, with no magic words or intent.
No: a warranty requires the seller to use the word “warrant,” “guarantee,” or something equivalent.
No: the seller didn't intend to warrant, and warranties are promises that require intent.
Only if the buyer proves the dealer knew the statement was false.
oe: Correct. Section 2-313(2) says the seller need not use formal words or have a specific intention to warrant. A specific statement of fact about the goods' construction is an express warranty.
Section 2-313(2) expressly rejects any formal-words requirement.
Intent is irrelevant. That's how § 2-313 blurs the line between representation and warranty.
Knowledge goes to fraud, not warranty. An express warranty is breached whenever the goods don't conform.
topic: Wk 2 · Express warranties — No magic words

q: A clothing boutique clerk tells a shopper, “That dress looks fantastic on you, and it's the best value in the store.” An art dealer tells a collector, “This is a beautiful painting by a very talented artist.” Do either of these statements create express warranties?
o: Neither: both are opinion, commendation, or statements of value, which are puffing.
Both: any statement a seller makes about the goods during the sale is an express warranty.
Only the art dealer's, because art sales involve expert sellers.
Only the boutique's “best value” statement, because value claims are measurable.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-313(2), an affirmation merely of the value of the goods or the seller's opinion or commendation doesn't create a warranty. “Looks fantastic,” “best value,” “beautiful,” and “talented” are subjective, general, and immeasurable (Problem 3-6(a)–(b)).
Section 2-313(2) carves out value, opinion, and commendation.
Expertise can matter, but “beautiful” and “talented” are still opinion.
Statements merely of value are expressly excluded from warranty.
topic: Wk 2 · Express warranties — Fact vs. opinion

q: An antiques dealer's tags describe a desk as “Queen Anne, circa 1720,” a vase as “Ming dynasty,” and a table as “antique.” A buyer purchases all three. Which best describes the dealer's statements?
o: Likely express warranties: specific descriptions of origin, period, and age.
They are puffing, because buyers know dealers exaggerate the age of antiques.
They are warranties only if the dealer wrote “guaranteed authentic” on the tags.
They are opinions, because only an expert appraiser could determine an antique's age.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-313(1)(b), a description that is part of the basis of the bargain creates a warranty that the goods conform. Trade usage gives these terms meaning; an open question is whether “Queen Anne” describes a period or merely a style (Problem 3-6(c)).
These are specific factual attributions, not general praise.
No formal words are needed.
A seller's specific attribution of origin is a statement of fact, even if verifying it takes expertise.
topic: Wk 2 · Express warranties — Descriptions as warranties

q: A sports memorabilia dealer sells a baseball labeled “the ball David Ortiz hit for a grand slam in Game 2 of the 2013 World Series.” An electronics retailer tells a buyer of a high-end receiver, “Replacement parts are readily available.” How are these statements best classified?
o: Both are likely express warranties: specific, measurable, verifiable affirmations of fact relating to the goods.
Both are puffing, because they're sales pitches typical of their industries.
The ball's label is a warranty, but the parts statement is puffing because it concerns the future.
Neither is a warranty unless the buyer asked for the information.
oe: Correct. The Ortiz provenance is a classic factual description (Problem 3-6(e)). The parts statement is a specific affirmation about the goods' usability, though one can ask whether a statement about the market “relates to the goods” (3-6(f)).
They're specific and verifiable, which points toward warranty.
Promises relating to the goods count, and the parts statement is specific and measurable.
Being made in response to an inquiry is one factor, not a requirement.
topic: Wk 2 · Express warranties — Specific provenance

q: Which of the following statements is the clearest example where courts have split on whether it is an express warranty or puffery?
o: A new-car dealer's statement that a model is “the safest car in its class.”
A clothing store clerk's statement that a dress “looks good on you.”
A tag stating that an engine produces “450 horsepower.”
A sample drawn from the bulk of a grain shipment shown to the buyer.
oe: Correct. Courts split (Gallagher v. WMK vs. Viking Yacht v. Composites One): superlatives are often puffery, but safety may be measurable through crash ratings (Problem 3-6(g)). “Seaworthy” is also split (Keith v. Buchanan vs. Sessa v. Riegle).
That's clear puffery.
That's a specific, measurable affirmation of fact, a clear warranty.
A sample made part of the basis of the bargain is a clear warranty that the whole conforms.
topic: Wk 2 · Express warranties — Close calls

q: A consumer selling her used washing machine on a local marketplace site tells a buyer, “It works great.” The machine stops spinning a week after the sale. Is the statement an express warranty?
o: It's a close call between a statement of fact and casual praise.
Clearly yes: any statement about the goods' condition is a warranty.
Clearly no: consumers selling used goods can't make express warranties.
Clearly no, because oral statements can't create warranties.
oe: Correct. Problem 3-6(d) (Petti v. Deridder) weighs specificity, the seller's knowledge, and how reasonable it was to rely on the statement. The fact-vs.-opinion factors include specific vs. general, measurable vs. immeasurable, and whether it was made in response to an inquiry.
General praise from a non-expert can be opinion; it isn't automatically a warranty.
Any seller, merchant or not, can make express warranties.
Oral statements can be warranties; writing is a factor, not a requirement.
topic: Wk 2 · Express warranties — The casual seller

q: A seller shows a buyer a bag of coffee beans drawn from the very lot to be sold and, separately, a polished display model of an espresso grinder that will be manufactured later. The contract doesn't mention either. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Both can, but a sample from the bulk carries the stronger presumption.
Only the sample creates a warranty, because models are only illustrations.
Neither creates a warranty unless the contract refers to it.
Both create warranties that are equally strong.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-313(1)(c), a sample or model made part of the basis of the bargain warrants that the whole of the goods will conform. Comment 6: a sample is drawn from the actual bulk and is presumed to describe the goods unless unmistakably denied; the presumption is weaker for a model offered when the goods aren't at hand.
Models can create warranties too; the presumption is just weaker.
A sample or model can become part of the basis of the bargain without a written reference.
Comment 6 distinguishes the strength of the presumption.
topic: Wk 2 · Express warranties — Sample vs. model

q: A seller's catalog states that a generator produces “7,500 running watts.” The buyer, a contractor, bought the generator and later admits he never read that line. The generator produces 5,000 watts. The seller argues there's no express warranty because the buyer didn't rely on the statement. What is the best answer?
o: Courts split: no reliance, strict reliance, or a rebuttable presumption.
The seller wins everywhere: a buyer must prove it read and relied on the statement.
The buyer wins everywhere: catalogs are always part of the contract.
The seller wins because the statement appeared in a catalog rather than in person.
oe: Correct. Comment 3 treats affirmations during the bargain as part of the description and requires “clear affirmative proof” to take them out. Courts divide three ways (Cole v. General Motors). Statements in the written contract don't need to be read (Holbrook; Samuel-Bassett).
That's only one of three approaches, and it conflicts with comment 3.
Courts don't agree, and some require reliance.
The medium doesn't matter; the debate is about reliance.
topic: Wk 2 · Express warranties — Basis of the bargain and reliance

q: A seller's bill of sale warrants that a painting is an authentic work by a famous artist. Before closing, the buyer heard from a gallery owner, a third party, that some experts questioned the attribution. The buyer closes without reserving rights. When the attribution is publicly challenged, the buyer sues on the warranty. Under Rogath v. Siebenmann, which is correct?
o: He may recover: he bought the seller's promise, and third-party knowledge doesn't waive it.
The buyer loses, because he knew of the doubts before closing and can't claim reliance.
The buyer loses unless he expressly reserved his rights, whatever the source of his knowledge.
The buyer wins only if the seller knew the painting was a forgery.
oe: Correct. Under New York law (CBS v. Ziff-Davis; Galli v. Metz), a buyer who closes knowing of facts disclosed by the seller that would breach the warranty waives the breach unless he preserves his rights. But knowledge from a third party doesn't; the buyer may have bought the warranty as insurance.
Knowledge alone doesn't defeat the warranty; its source matters.
Reservation is needed when the seller disclosed the problem, not a third party.
Warranty liability doesn't depend on the seller's knowledge.
topic: Wk 2 · Express warranties — Rogath v. Siebenmann

q: Variation: The seller himself told the buyer before closing that a major gallery had challenged the attribution, and the buyer closed without reserving any rights. What result?
o: He likely waived it by closing on seller-disclosed facts without reserving rights.
The buyer still wins, because a written warranty can never be waived.
The buyer still wins, because the seller's disclosure made the warranty even more specific.
The warranty never arose, because the seller's disclosure meant the buyer didn't rely on it.
oe: Correct. Galli v. Metz: where the seller discloses facts that would breach the warranty and the buyer closes anyway without reserving rights, the buyer waives the breach. In Rogath, a fact issue on exactly this point (who told the buyer) defeated summary judgment.
Under Galli, a buyer who closes with seller-disclosed knowledge waives unless he preserves rights.
Disclosure by the seller is what triggers the waiver rule.
The issue is waiver of the breach, not whether the warranty arose.
topic: Wk 2 · Express warranties — Seller-disclosed doubts
pre: A seller's bill of sale warrants that a painting is an authentic work by a famous artist. Before closing, the buyer heard from a gallery owner, a third party, that some experts questioned the attribution. The buyer closes without reserving rights. When the attribution is publicly challenged, the buyer sues on the warranty. Under Rogath v. Siebenmann, which is correct?

q: A buyer purchases an HVAC system. When it's delivered, the owner's manual in the box states: “This unit is free of defects in material and workmanship for one year from delivery.” Two years after delivery, a defect appears that existed from the start; the buyer discovers it then. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Likely a warranty despite timing; a future-performance warranty accrues on discovery.
The manual statement can't be a warranty, because it wasn't made before the contract was formed.
The manual is a warranty, and the claim accrued at tender, so the four-year period is measured from delivery regardless.
The manual statement is puffing, because “free of defects” is general praise.
oe: Correct. Comment 7 says timing doesn't matter: post-sale language can become part of the bargain as a modification needing no consideration, and manuals have been held warranties even if unread (Weinstat v. Dentsply). A warranty explicitly extending to future performance accrues when the breach is or should have been discovered (§ 2-725(2)).
Comment 7 rejects that timing objection.
That's the default rule; future-performance warranties accrue on discovery.
“Free of defects in material and workmanship for one year” is a specific promise.
topic: Wk 2 · Express warranties — Post-sale statements

q: Before buying an X3000 HVAC system, a building manager hears a sales rep say it produces “300,000 BTU per hour” and that he'd “be very happy with it,” and skims a brochure stating it runs “at less than 100 decibels.” Which statements are likely express warranties?
o: The BTU rating and the decibel figure, but not “very happy.”
All three, because each was made during the sales process.
Only the brochure figure, because oral statements by sales reps aren't warranties.
None, unless they were repeated in the signed contract.
oe: Correct. Specific, measurable figures are affirmations of fact, presumptively part of the basis of the bargain (cmt. 3). The buyer skimmed the brochure, which even satisfies a reliance-based view. “Very happy” is commendation. (Oral statements may face the parol evidence rule if a final writing exists.)
“Very happy” is opinion or commendation.
Oral statements can be warranties.
Pre-sale statements can be part of the basis of the bargain without being repeated.
topic: Wk 2 · Express warranties — Problem 3-7 sources

q: A 1930s cigarette ad says, “20,679 physicians say our brand is less irritating,” and another brand's ad says its cigars “give immediate relief in cases of asthma and bronchitis.” A third ad says simply, “It's toasted.” Which statements look most like express warranties rather than puffing?
o: The survey and asthma claims; “It's toasted” is puffing.
All three, because any statement in an advertisement is an express warranty.
None, because ads aren't directed at a particular buyer.
Only “It's toasted,” because it describes the manufacturing process.
oe: Correct. Specific health claims and claims backed by a stated survey look like affirmations of fact. Whether ads are part of the basis of the bargain turns on the reliance debate (did the buyer see them?).
General slogans remain puffing even in ads, and the basis-of-the-bargain issue remains.
Ads can create warranties; the open question is whether a buyer who never saw them can claim them.
It's vague; the specific health and survey claims are far more factual.
topic: Wk 2 · Express warranties — Advertising claims

q: Which of the following facts would most weaken a buyer's argument that a seller's statement became part of the basis of the bargain?
o: The statement was hedged, and the buyer could easily check it.
The seller was more of an expert about the goods than the buyer was.
The statement concerned a matter of objective importance to the buyer.
The price paid tends to support the buyer's claim about the quality promised.
oe: Correct. Factors supporting basis of the bargain include a plain and unambiguous statement on a matter of objective importance that the buyer couldn't easily ascertain, made by a seller more expert than the buyer, with nothing putting the buyer on guard. Hedging and easy verification cut the other way.
Seller expertise supports finding the statement part of the bargain.
That supports the buyer.
Price consistent with the claimed quality supports the buyer.
topic: Wk 2 · Express warranties — Basis-of-the-bargain factors

q: A signed record says only: “Seller sells Buyer one skid loader, $20,000.” It says nothing about delivery, and the parties have no prior dealings. Buyer insists Seller deliver it to Buyer's business; Seller insists Buyer pick it up. Buyer refuses to pick it up or pay, and Seller sues. What result?
o: Seller wins: the default place of delivery is Seller's place of business.
Buyer wins: when the contract is silent, the seller must deliver to the buyer's place of business.
Neither wins: there's no contract, because the parties never agreed on a delivery term.
Seller wins, but only because the price exceeds $500 and the record satisfies § 2-201.
oe: Correct. The parties intended to contract, and gap fillers supply a reasonably certain basis for a remedy (§ 2-204(3)). Under § 2-308(a), absent agreement, delivery is at the seller's place of business. Seller tenders by holding the loader at Buyer's disposition with notice (§ 2-503(1)), so Buyer breached (Problem 3-8(A)).
The default is the seller's place of business, not the buyer's.
Open terms don't defeat a contract if the parties intended one and there's a basis for a remedy.
Satisfying § 2-201 doesn't decide where delivery takes place; § 2-308 does.
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Gap fillers and delivery

q: A buyer accepted conforming goods and has refused to pay. Under the remedies map the course uses to decide whether a contract with open terms has a “reasonably certain basis for giving an appropriate remedy,” what is the seller's basic remedy?
o: An action for the price (§ 2-709).
Contract price minus market price (§ 2-708).
Market price minus contract price (§ 2-713).
Value as warranted minus value as accepted (§ 2-714).
oe: Correct. The map: buyer fails to pay for accepted goods → price (§ 2-709); buyer wrongfully refuses conforming goods → contract minus market (§ 2-708); seller tenders nonconforming goods and buyer rejects → market minus contract (§ 2-713); buyer accepts nonconforming goods → value as warranted minus value as accepted (§ 2-714). That's why price, quantity, quality, and delivery terms matter most.
That measure applies when the buyer refuses to take conforming goods.
That's a buyer's measure after a seller's non-delivery or rightful rejection.
That's the buyer's measure for accepted nonconforming goods.
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — The remedies map

q: Three buyers purchase cameras from a camera store. Buyer 1's lens is scratched. Buyer 2 told the clerk she needed a battery that would last four hours on a hiking trip, and the clerk picked one that lasts one hour. Buyer 3's camera turns out to be stolen. Which warranties are most directly implicated?
o: 1: merchantability. 2: fitness for a particular purpose. 3: title.
Buyer 1: fitness. Buyer 2: merchantability. Buyer 3: title.
All three: merchantability, because each camera is defective in some way.
Buyer 1: express warranty. Buyer 2: fitness. Buyer 3: noninfringement.
oe: Correct. The slide's camera chart pairs ordinary-quality problems with merchantability, the buyer's particular communicated need with fitness, and ownership problems with title.
A scratched lens is about ordinary quality (merchantability); Buyer 2's need was particular (fitness).
Stolen goods implicate title, and a communicated special need implicates fitness.
No express statement is mentioned for Buyer 1, and a stolen camera is a title problem, not infringement.
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Camera chart

q: A buyer gives a seller exact technical specifications for valves; the seller's brochure separately described the valves in general terms as “suitable for all industrial uses.” The valves meet the specs but fail in the buyer's application. Under § 2-317, how are conflicting warranties resolved?
o: Read them as consistent if reasonable; otherwise technical specs control.
The general description always controls, because it was made by the seller.
Express warranties always displace all implied warranties, including fitness.
The court must choose the warranty most favorable to the buyer.
oe: Correct. Section 2-317 resolves by the parties' intention: (a) exact or technical specs displace an inconsistent sample, model, or general description; (b) a sample from an existing bulk displaces an inconsistent general description; (c) express warranties displace inconsistent implied warranties other than fitness.
Technical specifications displace an inconsistent general description.
Section 2-317(c) excludes fitness from that rule.
The test is the parties' intention, guided by the § 2-317 presumptions.
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Cumulation and conflicts

q: A law firm sells its used office copier to a neighboring business. The copier turns out to have a defective drum. The buyer sues for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability. What is the law firm's best defense?
o: It isn't a merchant with respect to copiers, so it made no implied warranty of merchantability.
It is a “practices” merchant, but merchantability requires both parties to be merchants.
The copier was used, and merchantability never applies to used goods.
Merchantability must be expressly stated in the contract to apply.
oe: Correct. Section 2-314 applies only if the seller is a merchant with respect to goods of that kind, a narrow, goods-based status (§ 2-104 cmt. 2). An isolated sale doesn't qualify, though good faith requires disclosing known material hidden defects (cmt. 3).
Merchantability depends only on the seller, and on goods-merchant status, not practices status.
Merchantability applies to used goods sold by a merchant, with a reduced standard.
It's implied by law unless excluded. The issue is that this seller isn't a goods merchant.
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Who makes merchantability

q: A university's purchasing office regularly buys lab equipment and signs supply contracts. Which rule could most plausibly treat the university as a merchant?
o: The firm-offer rule of § 2-205, which uses the broad “practices” sense of merchant.
The implied warranty of merchantability, if the university sells surplus microscopes once a year.
The implied warranty against infringement, if the university sells one microscope.
None, because nonprofit institutions can never be merchants.
oe: Correct. Comment 2 to § 2-104 identifies “practices” provisions—§§ 2-201(2), 2-205, 2-207, and 2-209—where almost anyone in business, even a bank or university acting in a mercantile capacity, is a merchant. Goods-merchant provisions, like § 2-314, require dealing in goods of that kind.
Section 2-314 requires a merchant with respect to goods of that kind; occasional surplus sales likely don't qualify.
Section 2-312(3) requires a merchant regularly dealing in goods of the kind.
Comment 2 says even universities can be merchants under the practices provisions.
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Practices vs. goods merchants

q: Which seller is LEAST likely to make an implied warranty of merchantability for the goods involved?
o: A decorator who finds an antique chandelier for a hotel client for a finder's fee.
A full-time accountant who makes stained-glass baubles and sells them at her own stall at a semi-annual crafts fair.
A car-rental company that sells the oldest cars in its fleet every four months.
A custom-home contractor that regularly buys and installs appliances and fixtures its clients choose.
oe: Correct. The warrantor must be the seller, and the decorator isn't the seller. The actual seller warrants only if it is a merchant in goods of that kind (Problem 3-9(d)).
She regularly makes and sells goods of that kind and holds herself out with skill; she's likely a merchant as to baubles (3-9(a)).
Regular, recurring sales point toward merchant status as to used cars, though courts split (3-9(b)).
It regularly acquires and supplies those goods, so it's arguably a merchant; the warranty applies to the goods even if services predominate (3-9(c)).
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Problem 3-9

q: A hardware store sells a sealed ladder made by a reputable manufacturer. A hidden weld defect, present when it left the factory, causes it to collapse. The store proves it couldn't have discovered the defect by any reasonable inspection. Is the store liable for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability?
o: Yes: implied warranties are strict liability, so ignorance is no defense.
No: a seller is liable only for defects it knew of or should have discovered.
No: only the manufacturer makes implied warranties for sealed goods.
Yes, but only if the buyer shows the store made an express statement about the weld.
oe: Correct. Implied warranties aren't based on negligence. The buyer must prove the warranty, the breach (a defect at the time of sale), and causation; the seller's care can bear on whether the warranty was broken, but ignorance of a defect isn't a defense.
That's a negligence standard. Warranty liability is strict.
The merchant seller makes the warranty to its buyer, even for sealed goods.
Merchantability is implied by law.
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Strict liability

q: A homeowner buys a new lawn mower from a dealer on May 1. It works fine for three weeks, then the ignition fails on the fourth use. The dealer argues the mower was merchantable when sold because it worked at first. What's the best analysis?
o: Early failure is evidence of a defect at sale; likely breach absent misuse.
No breach: goods that work at the time of sale are merchantable by definition.
No breach unless the buyer proves exactly which part was defective.
Breach regardless of cause, because any failure within a year is a breach.
oe: Correct. Merchantability is measured at tender (§ 2-725(2)), but a quick failure can show a latent defect then. Comment 13 lets the seller show the loss resulted from events after delivery (Problem 3-10(a); Gillespie v. Sears on misuse).
Merchantability looks to whether a defect existed at sale, which early failure can prove.
Circumstantial evidence can establish a defect.
The seller can avoid liability by proving misuse or a post-delivery cause.
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Early failure and misuse

q: A diner chokes on a bone in a salmon fillet at a restaurant and needs surgery. She sues for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Serving food is a sale; under reasonable expectation, a fillet should be boneless.
She can't recover, because serving food in a restaurant is a service, not a sale.
She wins under every test, because any bone makes fish unmerchantable.
She can recover only in negligence, because natural substances never support warranty claims.
oe: Correct. Section 2-314(1) treats serving food for value as a sale. Under Webster v. Blue Ship Tea Room's foreign-natural test, a natural fish bone isn't a breach. Under the reasonable-expectation test (Schafer v. JLC Food Systems), a consumer may reasonably expect a fillet, unlike chowder, to be free of bones (Problem 3-10(b)).
Section 2-314(1) expressly treats serving food or drink for value as a sale.
Under the foreign-natural test, natural bones don't breach.
That's one court's view (Mexicali Rose); the reasonable-expectation test allows warranty claims.
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Bones in fish

q: A weaver buys five lots of “Magenta No. 02” yarn and finds noticeable color differences between the lots. The seller shows that dye-lot variation is normal in the trade and that weavers know to buy a single dye lot for a project. The color within each lot is even. Has the seller breached the implied warranty of merchantability?
o: Likely no: variation within trade tolerances is permitted.
Yes: goods sold under one description must be identical in every unit.
Yes: the color difference makes the yarn unfit for its ordinary purpose.
No, because merchantability never covers color or appearance.
oe: Correct. Section 2-314(2)(d) measures evenness within the variations the agreement permits, and the agreement includes trade usage. The yarn also likely passes without objection in the trade (2)(a). Variation beyond trade tolerances or within a single lot would be a breach (Problem 3-10(c)).
The standard allows variations permitted by the agreement, including trade usage.
Weaving with single dye lots is the ordinary practice; the yarn is fit for that.
Appearance can matter; the result turns on trade tolerances.
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Even kind and quality

q: A new $30,000 car complies with all federal and state safety rules but is rated low by a consumer group for front-impact protection. In a high-speed head-on collision, the engine is pushed into the passenger compartment and the buyer is badly injured. The buyer said nothing special about safety when buying. Is there likely a breach of the implied warranty of merchantability?
o: Likely no: the car need be only minimally safe, not best in class.
Yes: a car that performs worse than competitors in crash tests is unmerchantable.
No: compliance with safety regulations conclusively establishes merchantability.
Yes: any car that fails to protect its occupants in a crash breaches the warranty.
oe: Correct. Problem 3-10(d): being below average isn't the same as unmerchantable. Compliance is strong but not conclusive evidence. The result could differ under fitness if the buyer had communicated a particular safety need (Problem 3-11(B)).
Merchantability requires minimal quality, not best-in-class performance.
Compliance is strong evidence, not conclusive.
Ordinary purposes include reasonable crashworthiness, not protection in every crash.
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Crashworthiness

q: A medical-supply retailer resells boxes of gloves labeled “Latex Free” by the manufacturer. A nurse with a latex allergy has a reaction because the gloves contain latex. The retailer argues it didn't make the label statement. Can the buyer recover from the retailer for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability?
o: Yes: merchantable goods must conform to their label.
No: only the manufacturer can be liable for label statements.
No: label statements are express warranties, which only the party who wrote them makes.
Yes, but only if the retailer knew the gloves contained latex.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-314(2)(f), a merchant reseller impliedly warrants that the goods conform to label statements, even if it doesn't make them as its own express warranties.
The retailer's implied warranty includes conformity to the label.
Even if the retailer didn't make an express warranty, § 2-314(2)(f) makes label conformity part of merchantability.
Warranty liability is strict.
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Label statements

q: A used-car dealer sells a six-year-old truck priced at the low end of the blue book. The engine fails the next day. Which statement best describes the implied warranty of merchantability?
o: It applies at a reduced level for used goods.
It doesn't apply, because merchantability covers only new goods.
It applies in full, exactly as for a new truck.
It applies only if the dealer gave a written warranty.
oe: Correct. Merchantability applies to used goods sold by a merchant, but only such obligation as is appropriate to second-hand goods (cmt. 3). The buyer's knowledge of use, extent of use, and price matter; price is an excellent index of the quality obligation (cmt. 7).
It applies to used goods sold by a merchant, at a reduced level.
The content is reduced for second-hand goods.
It's implied by law.
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Used goods

q: A homeowner buys a space heater from a retailer. It's defective and starts a fire that injures the homeowner's visiting friend. The state has enacted Alternative A of § 2-318. Can the friend sue the retailer for breach of warranty?
o: Yes: Alternative A covers guests in the buyer's home.
No: only the buyer, who is in privity with the seller, can sue for breach of warranty.
Yes, but only if the retailer didn't disclaim liability to third parties.
No: Alternative A covers only members of the buyer's family, not guests.
oe: Correct. Alternative A covers family, household members, and guests in the home with personal injuries. Alternative B reaches any natural person reasonably expected to use, consume, or be affected who is injured in person. Alternative C reaches any person reasonably expected to be affected, not limited to personal injury. The seller can't exclude or limit § 2-318.
Section 2-318 extends warranty protection beyond the buyer.
The seller may not exclude or limit the operation of § 2-318.
Alternative A includes guests in the home.
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Third-party beneficiaries

q: A homeowner tells a hardware clerk she needs paint for the interior of her swimming pool and asks what to buy. The clerk picks a product off the shelf. The paint peels within weeks of filling the pool. The store argues no fitness warranty arose because the clerk never said the paint would work in a pool. What result?
o: Yes: the seller knew the purpose and the buyer's reliance, and she relied.
No fitness warranty arose, because the clerk made no affirmation about the paint.
A fitness warranty arose only if the store is a merchant in paint.
No warranty arose, because the buyer's reliance on a clerk was unreasonable.
oe: Correct. Section 2-315 needs no affirmation by the seller. The four requirements: the buyer has a particular purpose, the seller has reason to know of it, the seller has reason to know of the buyer's reliance, and the buyer actually relies (Problem 3-11(A)).
Affirmations create express warranties. Fitness is implied from the purpose and reliance.
Fitness doesn't require a merchant seller, though it usually involves one.
Reasonable reliance isn't required, though wholly unreasonable reliance may mean the seller had no reason to know of it.
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Fitness for a particular purpose

q: A manufacturer orders 2,000 brackets from a supplier, providing complete, precise drawings and specifications. The brackets meet the specs but fail in the buyer's machine. Separately, another buyer insists on a particular brand of adhesive over the seller's suggestion, and it fails in her outdoor application. Did either seller make a fitness warranty?
o: Neither, because neither buyer relied on the seller's judgment.
Both: each seller knew the purpose for which the goods were bought.
Only the bracket supplier, because it manufactured the goods.
Only the adhesive seller, because it suggested a different brand.
oe: Correct. Precise and complete specs normally negate reliance (Action Group v. NanoStatics; § 2-316 cmt. 9). Brand insistence negates reliance too (cmt. 5), though a brand recommended by the seller doesn't.
Knowing the purpose isn't enough; the buyer must actually rely on the seller.
Supplying goods to the buyer's specs negates reliance.
The buyer rejected the suggestion and chose her own brand, so she didn't rely on the seller.
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Specs and brand insistence

q: A barge company buys tank barges equipped with heating coils, telling the seller it will use them to carry heavy petroleum products that must be heated. The seller argues there can't be a fitness warranty because carrying heated petroleum is a common use for heating-coil barges. Under Ingram River Equipment v. Pott Industries, which statement is correct?
o: The purpose needn't be unique, just different enough from customary use.
Fitness never applies to a use that others in the industry share.
Any stated use is a particular purpose, so a fitness warranty always arises when the buyer explains its plans.
Fitness applies only when the goods are specially manufactured.
oe: Correct. Ingram River held the buyer's use need not be one of a kind. Comment 2's example: shoes are ordinarily for walking, but a seller may know a pair is for mountain climbing.
Ingram River rejected a uniqueness requirement.
If the purpose is the goods' ordinary use, merchantability, not fitness, covers it.
Fitness can apply to stock goods selected for a particular purpose.
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Particular vs. ordinary purpose

q: A commuter tells a car dealer she drives winding two-lane mountain roads and needs a car that will keep her safe in a serious collision. The salesperson recommends a model, and she buys it. In a crash, it performs poorly, though it meets all regulations. Compared with a buyer who said nothing about safety, which statement is most accurate?
o: She likely has a fitness claim, having stated her need and relied.
She has no better claim, because safety is an ordinary purpose of every car.
She has no claim, because the car complied with safety regulations.
She has a fitness claim only if the dealer is the manufacturer.
oe: Correct. Merchantability asks about average expectations for ordinary use; fitness asks about the particular buyer's communicated needs. By recommending the car, the dealer created an inference it would meet those needs (Problem 3-11(B), contrasting 3-10(d)).
Her communicated, specific need and reliance on the recommendation create a fitness warranty.
Compliance is evidence for merchantability, not a defense to fitness.
Reliance usually limits fitness claims to the immediate seller, which is the dealer.
topic: Wks 2–3 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Merchantability vs. fitness

q: A retired teacher sells her neighbor a bicycle she bought at a flea market for $300. It turns out the bicycle was stolen from its owner a month before the flea-market sale, and the police return it to the owner. The teacher argues she isn't a merchant and didn't know it was stolen. Is she liable to her neighbor?
o: Yes: every seller, merchant or not, warrants that the title conveyed is good and its transfer rightful.
No: only merchants warrant title.
No: because she bought in good faith, she had voidable title and passed good title to her neighbor.
Yes, but only if she knew or should have known it was stolen.
oe: Correct. The title warranty in § 2-312(1) is made by all sellers. Someone who bought from a thief gets void title and can pass none (Problem 3-12(B)), so the warranty is breached regardless of the seller's knowledge.
Merchant status matters for merchantability and infringement, not title.
A thief has void title, not voidable title, and anyone downstream takes nothing.
Title warranty liability doesn't depend on knowledge.
topic: Wk 3 · Title & infringement — Title warranty: all sellers

q: Owner sells a necklace to Fraudster, who pays with a check that later bounces. Before Owner discovers the problem, Fraudster sells the necklace to Buyer, who pays fair value and has no idea of the fraud. Owner sues Buyer to get the necklace back. Who wins?
o: Buyer: Fraudster's voidable title let it pass good title to a good-faith buyer for value.
Owner: a person who obtains goods by fraud gets no title at all.
Owner: because the check bounced, the sale was a nullity from the start.
Buyer, but only if Fraudster was a merchant who deals in necklaces.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-403(1), a purchaser has voidable title even though delivery was in exchange for a check later dishonored. A good-faith purchaser for value takes good title (Problem 3-12(C)).
Fraud in a voluntary sale produces voidable title, unlike theft, which produces void title.
Section 2-403(1)(b) specifically covers dishonored checks.
Merchant status matters for entrustment, not for the voidable-title rule.
topic: Wk 3 · Title & infringement — Voidable vs. void title

q: Variation: Owner doesn't win, but sues Buyer anyway, and Buyer spends $8,000 defending its title. Buyer then sues Fraudster for breach of the warranty of title. What is the best argument for Buyer?
o: A colorable claim can breach the title warranty, and defense costs are recoverable.
None: because Buyer ended up with good title, there can be no breach.
Buyer may recover the fees only if Fraudster acted in bad faith.
Buyer may recover its fees in suing Fraudster, but not its fees defending against Owner.
oe: Correct. Comment 1 says the buyer should receive a title free of exposure to a lawsuit to protect it. Fees spent defending title are recoverable consequential damages, though not fees for suing the seller.
Most courts allow a colorable claim to breach the warranty.
Bad faith matters to how liberally notice rules are applied (cmt. 2), not to whether a colorable claim breaches.
It's the reverse: defense costs are recoverable consequential damages; fees for suing the seller aren't.
topic: Wk 3 · Title & infringement — Colorable claims
pre: Owner sells a necklace to Fraudster, who pays with a check that later bounces. Before Owner discovers the problem, Fraudster sells the necklace to Buyer, who pays fair value and has no idea of the fraud. Owner sues Buyer to get the necklace back. Who wins?

q: Owner leaves her watch for repair with a jeweler that also sells watches. The jeweler sells it to Buyer, a customer who pays the full retail price in good faith with no reason to suspect anything. Owner sues to recover the watch from Buyer. Who wins?
o: Buyer: the jeweler, entrusted with the watch, could pass Owner's title to an ordinary-course buyer.
Owner: a repair shop that sells customers' goods is a thief, and thieves pass no title.
Owner: entrustment applies only if Owner authorized the jeweler to sell the watch.
Buyer, but only if the jeweler gave Buyer a written warranty of title.
oe: Correct. Under § 2-403(2)–(3), the entruster who clothed the merchant with apparent authority bears the risk. A buyer in ordinary course (§ 1-201(b)(9)) takes the owner's title (Problem 3-12(E)).
Entrustment applies even if the merchant's disposition is larcenous (§ 2-403(3)).
Entrusting includes any delivery and acquiescence in possession, regardless of conditions.
Entrustment depends on the merchant's status and the buyer's ordinary-course purchase, not on a written warranty.
topic: Wk 3 · Title & infringement — Entrustment

q: Buyer contracts to buy a necklace from a jeweler and pays, but lets the jeweler keep it for a week to engrave it. Meanwhile, the jeweler sells and delivers the same necklace to Purchaser, a buyer in ordinary course. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Purchaser: Buyer entrusted the necklace by leaving it with the jeweler.
Buyer keeps the necklace, because Buyer paid first and title had already passed.
Purchaser takes good title only if Buyer had not yet paid.
Neither has title; the jeweler must return the purchase price to both.
oe: Correct. Entrusting includes acquiescence in retention of possession (§ 2-403(3)). Purchaser, a buyer in ordinary course, takes good title. Buyer sues the jeweler for non-delivery or conversion (Problem 3-12(F)).
Article 2 de-emphasizes title, and entrustment lets the jeweler transfer Buyer's rights to Purchaser.
Payment doesn't change the entrustment analysis.
Purchaser takes good title under § 2-403(2).
topic: Wk 3 · Title & infringement — Entrustment by a buyer

q: A seller ships goods to a buyer under a shipment contract. The buyer's creditor seizes the goods in transit, and the parties dispute who owned them. Which statement best describes the role of “title” under Article 2?
o: Article 2 rules mostly ignore title, but title matters elsewhere.
Risk of loss and the buyer's remedies depend entirely on who has title.
Title is irrelevant for every purpose once Article 2 applies.
Title passes when the contract is signed, whatever the delivery terms.
oe: Correct. Section 2-401 says each provision applies irrespective of title unless it refers to title. Title still matters for creditors, insurance, taxes, and bankruptcy. In a shipment contract it passes at shipment (§ 2-401(2)(a)); in a destination contract, on tender at the destination.
Risk of loss turns on tender, control, and breach (§§ 2-509, 2-510), not title.
Title still matters outside Article 2.
Absent agreement, title passes on the seller's completed delivery performance.
topic: Wk 3 · Title & infringement — Title de-emphasized

q: A garage-sale seller sells a used drone. A patent holder later claims the drone's design infringes its patent and demands royalties from the buyer. Separately, an electronics distributor that regularly sells drones sells identical new drones to a store, which receives the same demand. Which seller warranted against infringement?
o: Only the distributor, a merchant regularly dealing in drones.
Both, because every seller warrants that its goods are free of third-party claims.
Neither, because infringement is a matter of patent law, not sales law.
Only the garage-sale seller, because it sold used goods with unknown history.
oe: Correct. Section 2-312(3) imposes the warranty on merchants regularly dealing in goods of the kind; a sale by a non-dealer carries no implied infringement warranty (cmt. 3).
The general title warranty doesn't cover infringement; § 2-312(3) is limited to dealers.
Section 2-312(3) addresses infringement claims as a matter of warranty.
It's the dealer, not the casual seller, who warrants against infringement.
topic: Wk 3 · Title & infringement — Noninfringement

q: A merchant manufacturer makes 10,000 phone cases to a buyer's detailed design specifications. A design-patent holder sues the manufacturer for infringement based on the buyer's design. Who bears the risk?
o: The buyer, which must indemnify a seller that followed its specs.
The manufacturer, because merchants regularly dealing in goods always warrant against infringement.
The patent holder, because the buyer's design was independently created.
They share the risk equally under Article 2's gap fillers.
oe: Correct. Section 2-312(3)'s exception flips the indemnity: the buyer tacitly represents that the seller will be safe manufacturing to its specs (cmt. 3).
The specification exception shifts the risk to the buyer.
The patent holder's claim is a matter of patent law; between buyer and seller, the buyer bears it.
The statute allocates it to the buyer who supplied the specs.
topic: Wk 3 · Title & infringement — Buyer's specifications

q: A retailer bought 5,000 T-shirts from a merchant supplier. A company sends the retailer a cease-and-desist letter claiming the shirts' design infringes its trademark and threatens suit. The retailer pulls the shirts and sues the supplier for breach of the warranty against infringement. Must the retailer prove the trademark claim is valid?
o: No: it need only show a substantial claim that clouds its use.
Yes: the warranty is breached only if the goods actually infringe.
No: any claim at all, even a frivolous one, breaches the warranty.
Yes, and the retailer must also have been sued and lost.
oe: Correct. Sun Coast Merchandise v. Myron requires a substantial claim with a significant adverse effect, not proof of validity. Pacific Sunwear's more lenient test excludes only frivolous claims. Eviction isn't required (cmt. 4).
Buyers need not prove validity; the claim's substantial shadow is enough.
Even the lenient Pacific Sunwear test excludes frivolous claims.
Comment 4 says eviction isn't required; the remedy arises on receipt of notice of infringement.
topic: Wk 3 · Title & infringement — Proving an infringement claim

q: A buyer is sued by a patent holder claiming that machinery the buyer purchased infringes its patent. The buyer defends the suit for a year without telling the seller, then loses and sues the seller on the warranty against infringement. What is the seller's best defense?
o: The buyer didn't notify the seller of the suit within a reasonable time.
The warranty against infringement expires one year after delivery.
The buyer should have settled rather than litigated.
Infringement warranties can be enforced only by the patent holder.
oe: Correct. Section 2-607(3)(b) requires a buyer sued for infringement to notify the seller within a reasonable time after receiving notice of the litigation, or be barred from any remedy over.
No such period exists; the issue is the notice requirement.
Article 2 doesn't require settlement; it requires timely notice.
The buyer is the beneficiary of the seller's warranty.
topic: Wk 3 · Title & infringement — Notice of infringement suit

q: A cabinet maker signs a five-year contract to buy 50,000 square feet of particle board per year at $1 per square foot. In year four, customer demand shifts to hardwood, and the cabinet maker tells the seller it will buy only 20,000 square feet that year. The seller objects. Can the cabinet maker reduce its purchases?
o: No: it's a fixed-quantity contract, so cutting purchases needs a modification.
Yes: a buyer may reduce purchases in good faith when its actual needs decline.
Yes: a market shift makes performance commercially impracticable under § 2-615.
Yes, if the reduction isn't unreasonably disproportionate to prior years.
oe: Correct. Problem 4-1(a): the contract states a fixed quantity, not requirements. Buying only 20,000 square feet is a breach unless the seller agrees to a modification. Excuse arguments are weak, because a market shift is exactly the risk a fixed contract allocates.
That's the rule for requirements contracts, and this contract states a fixed quantity.
A change in demand is a market event, not a contingency that excuses performance.
The disproportion test applies to output and requirements terms, not fixed quantities.
topic: Wk 3 · Quantity & price — Fixed quantity

q: A cabinet maker agrees to buy its annual “requirements” of particle board at $1 per square foot, with no estimate, minimum, or maximum. Its requirements were 25,000, 32,500, and 35,000 square feet in the first three years. In year four, the market price rises to $1.15, and the buyer demands 60,000 square feet, its plant's full capacity. What is the seller's best argument?
o: The demand is disproportionate to prior years and looks like bad faith.
Requirements contracts without an estimate are void for indefiniteness.
A buyer may never increase its requirements beyond the prior year's amount.
The seller is bound to supply any quantity the buyer actually uses.
oe: Correct. Without an estimate, § 2-306(1) compares the demand to normal or comparable prior requirements. The Orange & Rockland factors (size of the increase, whether the seller could anticipate it, the market-over-contract spread, fortuity, and the reason) all cut against the buyer, and demanding capacity rather than actual needs looks opportunistic (Problem 4-1(b)).
Requirements terms are valid; the absence of an estimate means prior requirements become the benchmark.
Normal, good-faith growth is allowed; only unreasonably disproportionate amounts are barred.
Even actual requirements are limited by the disproportion test.
topic: Wk 3 · Quantity & price — Requirements in a rising market

q: A buyer has a five-year contract for all of its widget requirements; it bought 90,000 in year one and 100,000 in year two. In year three it lands a huge new customer and honestly needs 400,000 widgets. Must the seller supply them?
o: No: the demand is in good faith but unreasonably disproportionate to prior requirements.
Yes: as long as the requirements are genuine and in good faith, the seller must supply them.
No, because a requirements buyer acts in bad faith whenever it grows its business.
Yes, because without an estimate, there is no limit on requirements.
oe: Correct. Problem 4-2(A): good faith and the disproportion limit are separate tests. An honest need four times the prior level, beyond what the seller could reasonably anticipate, can still be refused.
Good faith is necessary but not sufficient; the quantity also must not be unreasonably disproportionate.
Normal good-faith growth is allowed; the problem here is disproportion.
Prior requirements supply the benchmark when there's no estimate.
topic: Wk 3 · Quantity & price — Two separate limits

q: Variation: In year three, the market price rises above the contract price, and the buyer orders 110,000 widgets, in line with its history. But the buyer plans to resell the extra 10,000 on the open market at a profit rather than use them. Must the seller supply the full 110,000?
o: No: proportionate, but not an actual good-faith requirement.
Yes: the order is in line with prior years, so the disproportion test is satisfied.
Yes: the buyer may use or dispose of the goods however it chooses once it pays.
No, because a requirements buyer may never resell any goods.
oe: Correct. Problem 4-2(B): requirements mean actual needs arising in good faith. Ordering to resell in a rising market (or, in a falling market, buying elsewhere and ordering less) is bad faith even if the number looks normal.
Satisfying one test doesn't satisfy the other.
The quantity term covers actual requirements, not goods for speculative resale.
The problem is ordering beyond genuine needs to profit on resale, not resale as such.
topic: Wk 3 · Quantity & price — Proportionate but bad faith
pre: A buyer has a five-year contract for all of its widget requirements; it bought 90,000 in year one and 100,000 in year two. In year three it lands a huge new customer and honestly needs 400,000 widgets. Must the seller supply them?

q: A buyer with a requirements contract at a fixed price of $1 sees its needs collapse from 35,000 units to 5,000 in a recession, while the market price falls to 90 cents. The seller suspects the buyer is filling the rest of its needs elsewhere at the lower price. Which statement best describes the law on decreases?
o: Courts split on whether disproportion limits decreases; diversion is bad faith.
A requirements buyer may never decrease its purchases below the first year's level.
Decreases are always allowed, because the disproportion test applies only to increases.
The buyer must keep buying the prior year's quantity until the contract ends.
oe: Correct. Empire Gas and HML apply good faith only; Simcala applies both tests. Comment 2: a shutdown for lack of orders may be permissible, but one merely to curtail losses isn't. Buying elsewhere at the lower market price would breach good faith (Problem 4-1(c)).
Good-faith reductions, even to zero, can be permissible.
Some courts apply the disproportion test to decreases too.
That treats the contract as a fixed-quantity deal, which it isn't.
topic: Wk 3 · Quantity & price — Decreases in requirements

q: Which statement about output and requirements contracts is correct?
o: Section 2-306 interprets agreed terms only, and such terms satisfy § 2-201.
When a contract omits quantity, § 2-306 supplies the buyer's reasonable requirements.
A requirements contract fails the statute of frauds because the record doesn't state a number.
A non-exclusive requirements contract is always void as illusory.
oe: Correct. Quantity is the term least suited to gap filling; § 2-306 governs only agreed output or requirements terms. Such a commitment satisfies § 2-201's quantity requirement (PMC Corp.). An estimate or a fixed percentage can answer mutuality concerns in non-exclusive deals.
Section 2-306 never implies a quantity term.
A requirements term is a quantity term for § 2-201 purposes.
Some courts worry about mutuality, but a fixed percentage or an estimate can save it.
topic: Wk 3 · Quantity & price — Interpreting the quantity term

q: A manufacturer appoints a distributor as its exclusive seller of a new kitchen appliance in a three-state region. The contract is silent on the distributor's sales efforts. The distributor makes almost no effort to sell the appliance. What, if anything, has the distributor breached?
o: The implied duty to use best efforts to promote the goods.
Nothing, because the contract didn't require any sales effort.
The implied warranty of merchantability, by failing to market the goods properly.
Only the duty of good faith, which requires minimal effort.
oe: Correct. Section 2-306(2): unless otherwise agreed, exclusive dealing obliges the seller to use best efforts to supply the goods and the buyer to use best efforts to promote their sale.
Section 2-306(2) implies best efforts in exclusive dealing.
Merchantability concerns goods' quality, not a distributor's sales efforts.
Section 2-306(2) imposes the more demanding best-efforts standard.
topic: Wk 3 · Quantity & price — Exclusive dealing

q: On February 1, a buyer and seller sign a record for 1,000 sacks of potatoes, delivery March 15, price “to be agreed at delivery.” On March 15, the seller demands $15 per sack when the market is $12; the buyer refuses and buys elsewhere at $13. The seller argues there was never a contract. What result?
o: Buyer likely wins: the price is a reasonable price at delivery, about $12.
The seller wins: an agreement to agree on price is unenforceable.
The seller wins: when parties fail to agree on price, the seller may fix it.
The buyer wins, and the price is the $7 market price on February 1.
oe: Correct. Section 2-305(1)(b): if the price is left to be agreed and the parties fail to agree, the price is a reasonable price at delivery, about $12. The buyer may recover its cover costs, about $1 per sack plus incidental damages (§ 2-712). The seller wins only if the parties intended not to be bound without agreement (§ 2-305(4)) (Problem 4-3(a)).
Comment 1 rejects the rule that an agreement to agree is unenforceable when the parties intend to be bound.
The seller may fix the price only if the contract gives it that power; here the price was left to agreement.
The reasonable price is measured at the time for delivery, not at contracting.
topic: Wk 3 · Quantity & price — Price to be agreed

q: A potato contract sets the price as “the Chicago Board of Trade price on March 15.” The Board shuts down on March 14 due to a fraud scandal; its last quote, on March 13, was $12. The seller tenders on March 15 and demands $12. The buyer rejects the potatoes, buys elsewhere at $11, and argues there was no contract. What result?
o: Seller likely wins: a reasonable price applies, and $12 is strong evidence.
The buyer wins: the price mechanism failed, so there's no contract.
The buyer wins: the reasonable price is $11, the price it actually paid elsewhere.
The seller wins and may recover $15 per sack, its asking price on any other day.
oe: Correct. Section 2-305(1)(c) keeps the contract alive if the parties intended one. If $12 is reasonable (the $11 purchase is contrary evidence), the seller's tender was proper, and the buyer breached by rejecting (Problem 4-3(b)).
Failure of an agreed standard leads to a reasonable price, not no contract, if the parties intended to be bound.
The buyer's purchase is some evidence, but the last market quote is strong evidence of the reasonable price.
The seller gets a reasonable price, not whatever it chooses.
topic: Wk 3 · Quantity & price — Failed market standard

q: A contract prices potatoes “as set by an independent third party agreed to by Buyer and Seller.” At delivery, the buyer refuses to agree to or name any third party and refuses the potatoes. The market is $13. What are the seller's options?
o: Cancel, or fix a reasonable price itself, because the buyer caused the failure.
None: the price mechanism failed, so there's no contract.
The seller must ask a court to appoint an appraiser to set the price.
The seller may set any price it chooses, because the buyer forfeited its rights.
oe: Correct. Section 2-305(3) gives the non-faulting party that option; the buyer's refusal to cooperate is also a breach (cmt. 5; § 2-311(3)) (Problem 4-3(c)). Things would differ if a particular expert's valuation were an essential condition (cmt. 4).
Section 2-305(3) addresses exactly this failure caused by one party.
The statute lets the seller cancel or fix a reasonable price itself.
The seller may fix only a reasonable price.
topic: Wk 3 · Quantity & price — Fault in fixing the price

q: A collector agrees to sell a unique painting at a price “to be determined by Dr. Lena Ortiz,” a renowned expert both parties trust. Dr. Ortiz dies before setting the price, and neither party is at fault. Which result is most likely?
o: Possibly no contract, if the expert was essential; then restitution.
The price is automatically a reasonable price at the time for delivery.
The seller may set the price in good faith.
The buyer must pay the painting's appraised value at the time of contracting.
oe: Correct. Comment 4: when a specific expert's valuation is essential (as with a trusted expert valuing a unique painting), failure of that expert may mean no contract. Section 2-305(4) then requires restitution. Contrast a named expert grading cotton, where a substitute will do.
That applies to failed market or third-party standards unless the particular expert was essential.
The contract didn't give the seller that power.
No rule supplies that price; the issue is whether a contract survives at all.
topic: Wk 3 · Quantity & price — Essential expert

q: A fuel supplier's franchise agreement requires dealers to buy gasoline at a price the supplier sets. Its prices are within the range charged by competitors, but internal memos show the supplier set them to drive certain franchisees out of business so it could take over their stations. In a jurisdiction following Mathis v. Exxon, has the supplier breached its duty under § 2-305(2)?
o: Yes: subjective bad faith defeats the safe harbor.
No: a price within competitors' range is in good faith, regardless of motive.
No: a party that sets the price can set any price it likes.
Yes: any posted price is presumptively in bad faith.
oe: Correct. Section 2-305(2) requires a party fixing the price to do so in good faith. Mathis read comment 3's “normal case” language to require both honesty in fact and commercial reasonableness, upholding a jury verdict for the franchisees.
That's the majority view (Shell v. HRN; Autry v. BP), which Mathis rejected.
A price fixed by one party must be fixed in good faith.
Posted and market prices are generally within comment 3's safe harbor.
topic: Wk 3 · Quantity & price — Seller-set price

q: Variation: The same case is in a jurisdiction following Shell Oil v. HRN and Autry Petroleum v. BP. The supplier applies the price uniformly to all similarly situated dealers. What result?
o: The supplier likely wins; motive is irrelevant to the safe harbor.
The supplier loses, because good faith always includes a subjective element.
The supplier loses, because a party fixing the price owes fiduciary duties.
The supplier wins, but only if it proves the dealers were unprofitable anyway.
oe: Correct. The majority view says that letting allegations of bad motive defeat the safe harbor would inject uncertainty. The drafters' main concern was price discrimination.
The majority view looks only at commercial reasonableness and non-discrimination for posted prices.
No fiduciary duty arises from § 2-305(2).
The franchisees' profitability isn't the test.
topic: Wk 3 · Quantity & price — The majority safe harbor
pre: A fuel supplier's franchise agreement requires dealers to buy gasoline at a price the supplier sets. Its prices are within the range charged by competitors, but internal memos show the supplier set them to drive certain franchisees out of business so it could take over their stations. In a jurisdiction following Mathis v. Exxon, has the supplier breached its duty under § 2-305(2)?

q: A contract for 200 chairs says nothing about who performs first. On the delivery date, the seller stands ready but doesn't tender the chairs, and the buyer stands ready but doesn't tender payment. Neither does anything more. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Tenders are concurrent conditions, so neither party breached.
The seller breached, because the seller always performs first under Article 2.
The buyer breached, because payment is due when the contract is formed.
Both breached, so each owes the other damages.
oe: Correct. Section 2-301 states the basic obligations; §§ 2-507(1) and 2-511(1) make the tenders concurrent conditions. If one party fails to tender, the other is excused; if both fail, neither breached (they've implicitly terminated).
Article 2 doesn't make the seller go first by default; the parties often agree that it will.
Payment is due on receipt of goods (§ 2-310(a)), not at formation.
When neither tenders, neither is in breach.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Tender, delivery & payment — Concurrent conditions

q: A seller agrees to sell 100 bushels of wheat at $4 per bushel and is to tender before the buyer pays. The seller phones that the wheat is ready. The buyer arrives with trucks and finds only 95 bushels, and the auger normally used to load trucks is broken. Has the seller made a proper tender?
o: No: a short, nonconforming tender; the auger depends on who must load.
Yes: 95% of the goods is substantial performance, and the buyer must accept and seek a price reduction.
Yes: the shortage is irrelevant, because the buyer may simply take the 95 bushels and pay for them.
No, but only because of the broken auger; the shortage is too small to matter.
oe: Correct. Conforming goods are required (§ 2-106(2)), and § 2-307 requires a single delivery of all the goods, so the buyer may reject under § 2-601. The buyer generally furnishes facilities for receipt (§ 2-503(1)(b)), but trade usage or course of dealing could put loading on the seller (Problem 4-4(a)(1)).
Outside installment contracts, Article 2 uses perfect tender, not substantial performance.
The buyer may choose to accept, but the tender wasn't proper.
Any shortfall makes the tender nonconforming under the perfect tender rule.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Tender, delivery & payment — Short delivery and loading

q: Same wheat contract. The seller calls the buyer and says, “Your wheat is ready. Pick it up within two hours or I'll sell it to someone else.” The buyer's facility is 60 miles away. Is this a proper tender?
o: Probably not: two hours isn't a reasonable period to take possession.
Yes: notice plus readiness to deliver is all that tender requires.
Yes, because the seller may set any pickup window it likes when the contract is silent.
No, because a seller must always deliver to the buyer's location.
oe: Correct. Section 2-503(1)(a) requires tender at a reasonable hour and a reasonable holding period, which depends on distance and trade practice (Problem 4-4(a)(3)).
Tender also requires holding the goods for a reasonable period.
The default is a reasonable period, not one the seller chooses unilaterally.
The default place is the seller's place of business; the problem is the time window.
topic: Wks 4–5 · Tender, delivery & payment — Holding period

q: Same wheat contract, which says nothing about place. The seller tells the buyer to pick up the wheat at the seller's warehouse 300 miles from both the buyer's business and the seller's offices. At contracting, the buyer didn't know the wheat was there. Is this a proper tender?
