oe: Correct. Good faith limits overpaying with someone else's money. Vance likely recovers no more than the $10 a chair a reasonable buyer would have lost, or a court may deny § 2-712 treatment and go to § 2-713.
Cover must be a reasonable purchase made in good faith.
No herculean search is required, but this isn't a close case.
There's no per se bar; the markup is the problem.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Overpaying on cover

q: Under a contract for a $40,000 car with a $500 entertainment system, the dealer repudiates. Ana buys the same make and model for $42,000. Hers has heated seats and a moon roof (worth $1,000 together) but no entertainment system. What is the best estimate of her cover differential?
o: $1,500: $2,000, less $1,000 for extras, plus $500 for the missing system.
$2,000, because differences in features are ignored.
$1,000, because extras are deducted but missing items aren't added.
$2,500, because only the missing system is taken into account.
oe: Correct. Start at cover minus contract and adjust to reach the expectancy, assuming the car is a reasonable substitute and the sticker price reflects the extras.
Courts adjust to avoid over- or under-compensation.
The missing system is part of the lost bargain.
The extras are a benefit she must account for.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Different features both ways

q: Mid-term, Allied refuses to deliver unless Pryor pays $5 more per unit. Pryor has no alternative, pays under protest and later sues for the $5. The text flags which open question?
o: Whether that purchase is cover or an agreed modification with no breach.
Whether Pryor's protest makes the whole contract void.
Whether Article 2 forbids buying cover from the breaching seller.
Whether Pryor had to give 30 days' notice of its protest.
oe: Correct. If it's a modification, there may be no breach. Section 2-209 good faith and the Roth Steel framework matter, and § 1-308 lets a party reserve rights. If Pryor had refused the offer, was that a failure to mitigate? The text leaves these open.
Protest doesn't void anything; it may preserve rights (§ 1-308).
Article 2 has no express bar, which is why the question is open.
No such notice rule exists.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Covering with the breacher

q: Under a contract for delivery on Oct. 1, the seller repudiates on July 1. The buyer doesn't cover. Prices rise steadily. The buyer sues under § 2-713, and the parties dispute the date of "learned of the breach." Which statement fairly reflects the authorities the text cites?
o: Courts differ: the performance date or a reasonable time after repudiation.
All courts use the repudiation date, because the statute says so.
All courts use the first day of trial.
The contract date controls, since the risk was priced then.
oe: Correct. Both are cited at p. 275 n.17. A third reading, outside class materials, uses the date the buyer learned of the repudiation.
The statute doesn't resolve it, and the courts are split.
No cited court uses the trial date.
No cited court does so.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Learned of the breach after repudiation

q: A 10-year gravel supply contract is repudiated by the seller in year 5. Trial is in year 7. What is the proper way to price the remaining years under § 2-713?
o: Section 2-723(1) reaches only performance not yet due at trial.
Section 2-723(1) governs all of the remaining years.
Section 2-723(1) applies even if trial comes after the term ends.
Only year 5 can be recovered, since the repudiation occurred then.
oe: Correct. Performance due before trial (years 6-7) isn't within § 2-723(1). Years 8-10, not yet due, use the price when the buyer learned of the repudiation.
It doesn't reach performance already due at trial.
Not after the time for performance has passed.
Damages reach the rest of the term.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Long-term supply, § 2-723

q: Gantry contracts to buy a $100,000 press. Gantry would have spent $1,000 modifying its floor to fit it. The seller repudiates before the work starts, and Gantry buys a $104,000 press that needs no modification. What are Gantry's direct damages?
o: $4,000, because savings are ignored in cover.
$5,000, because the $1,000 is added.
$1,000, the amount saved.
oe: Correct. Both formulas deduct costs the buyer avoided, so damages match the expectancy.
Section 2-712(2) subtracts expenses saved.
Savings are subtracted.
That isn't the formula.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Expenses saved

q: Coastal Charters orders a replacement engine from Marine Supply, stating nothing about its bookings. After contracting, Coastal phones to say the boat must be running by June 1 for a $60,000 charter. The engine comes a month late. Coastal sues for the lost charter. What is the seller's best defense?
o: It had no reason to know of the charter at contracting.
Lost profits are never recoverable under Article 2.
Coastal had to prove that it acted in bad faith.
Coastal's loss exceeds the price of the engine.
oe: Correct. Section 2-715(2)(a) requires reason to know "at the time of contracting." Notice afterward is too late.
A buyer's lost profits are classic consequential damages.
Bad faith isn't an element.
Consequential damages can far exceed the price.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — When reason to know is tested

q: Keystone Builders has a cost-plus contract with a developer. When a window supplier repudiates a $70,000 order, Keystone covers at $90,000 and passes the extra $20,000 to the developer. The supplier argues Keystone lost nothing. What does Problem 7-9 and KGM Harvesting suggest?
o: KGM allowed cover damages, though the issue tests § 2-712 against § 1-305.
A pass-through always bars cover damages.
The developer, not Keystone, must bring the § 2-712 claim.
Keystone may recover from both the supplier and the developer.
oe: Correct. The casebook cites KGM only (p. 280). The cost-plus pattern shows the formula's tension with the expectancy principle.
The cited case went the other way.
The developer isn't a party to the supply contract.
That would be a double recovery.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Pass-through cost plus

q: Blue Sky needed 200,000 gallons of fuel at $5.00 after its seller repudiated. Over the next month it bought 600,000 gallons in many lots: 100,000 at $5.20 and 100,000 at $5.40 first, later lots at $5.80. What is the likely cover?
o: The earliest purchases: $60,000 above contract.
The most expensive 200,000 gallons, since the buyer may choose.
The average price of all 600,000 gallons.
None, because it bought more fuel than it needed.
oe: Correct. A buyer that makes several purchases must show which ones replaced the breached contract: 100,000 × $0.20 + 100,000 × $0.40 = $60,000.
The buyer can't cherry-pick the highest lots.
Most of those purchases weren't substitutes for this contract.
Over-buying doesn't void cover; it just requires matching.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Multiple purchases

q: Under a $5,000 contract for ten wood desks F.O.B. Phoenix (freight about $500), with $100 paid down, the seller writes, "We can't do wood. We can ship a different model at $800 each." The buyer writes, "Cancel the order and refund my deposit," then buys ten metal desks for $6,000 delivered. Which is correct?
o: It's a repudiation, and cover damages are $500 plus the $100 refund.
The letter is a counteroffer, so no breach occurred.
The buyer's refusal of the $800 model forfeits damages.
Cover damages are $1,000, because the freight is the seller's cost.
oe: Correct. Cover $6,000 minus contract $5,000 = $1,000, less $500 freight saved (delivered price). "Cancel... refund" doesn't waive damages. A fight over whether metal is an upgrade is possible.
The seller refused to perform as agreed, which is a repudiation.
A buyer needn't accept a modification at a higher price.
Under F.O.B. Phoenix the buyer would have paid freight, so it's an expense saved.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Different model offer

q: Same facts, but the buyer covers with suitable desks at $4,000 delivered. Which is correct?
o: No cover damages, but the $100 refund and provable other losses.
The buyer owes the seller the $1,000 it saved.
The buyer may claim § 2-713 if the market is higher.
The buyer loses the $100 refund, having done better.
oe: Correct. Having covered it can't switch to § 2-713, unless the desks aren't a true substitute. It is better off on price, and the seller gets no credit claim for that.
The formula never runs in the seller's favor.
Having covered, it can't switch.
Section 2-711(1) gives it back regardless.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Cheaper cover
pre: Under a $5,000 contract for ten wood desks F.O.B. Phoenix (freight about $500), with $100 paid down, the seller writes, "We can't do wood. We can ship a different model at $800 each." The buyer writes, "Cancel the order and refund my deposit," then buys ten metal desks for $6,000 delivered. Which is correct?

q: Under a contract for 5,000 lb of lobster at $10/lb F.O.B. Bar Harbor, for July 1 delivery, the seller repudiates on June 1. On June 15 the buyer's Long Island restaurant buys prime rib. Bar Harbor lobster prices: June 1, $12; June 15, $13; July 1, $14. Long Island prices are higher. Under the commercially-reasonable-time approach, treating June 15 as that time, what are direct damages?
o: $20,000: the performance date always controls.
The prime rib price minus $10/lb, as the buyer covered.
$15,000 plus the Long Island price premium.
oe: Correct. Prime rib isn't a reasonable substitute, so § 2-713 applies at the place for tender. The date rule gives $10,000 (June 1), $15,000 (June 15) or $20,000 (July 1).
That's one approach; the question specifies another.
Prime rib isn't a reasonable substitute for lobster.
The place for tender is Bar Harbor, so Long Island prices are out.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Lobster not cover

q: Broker buys 100,000 gallons at $2.50 F.O.B. New Orleans and has a fixed resale at $2.70 to Customer. Seller repudiates when the market is $4.50 in New Orleans. Customer waives all claims against Broker. Broker's real lost profit is about $14,500. Which statement is right?
o: The formula gives $200,000, and courts split on capping it at actual loss.
Article 2 expressly caps all buyers at actual resale profit.
Broker recovers both the $200,000 and the $14,500.
A broker has no § 2-713 claim, as it didn't plan to use the goods.
oe: Correct. H-W-H Cattle and Allied Canners are on one side, TexPar and Tongish on the other (all cited only, p. 280). The first pair caps recovery near actual loss under § 1-305; the second keeps the market measure.
The statute has no such cap, and the cases split.
That stacks the recovery.
Section 2-713 applies to brokers.
topic: Wk 8 · XVIII · Buyer's damages: cover, market, incidental & consequential (§§ 2-712, 2-713, 2-715, 2-723) — Broker fixed resale

q: Harbor Grill rejects a load of defective freezers. Its lawyer's letter says Harbor has "rescinded and repudiated the contract." The seller replies that Harbor has now breached. What is the correct characterization of a proper rejection?
o: It refuses the seller's tender but does not end the contract or repudiate it.
It automatically cancels the contract and discharges the seller's duties.
It counts as a repudiation that gives the seller immediate § 2-703 remedies.
It rescinds the sale, so the buyer loses any claim for damages.
oe: Correct. Rejection is a refusal of the tender. The contract survives, which is why cure may still be possible. The letter's loose wording could cause trouble and should be avoided.
Cancellation is a separate step under § 2-711(1). Rejection alone doesn't end the seller's obligations.
A rightful rejection isn't a repudiation; the seller is the party in breach.
Rejection and damages are compatible (§ 2-711; see also § 2-721).

She loses unless she suffered a personal injury.
She may proceed, but only on the express warranty.
oe: Correct. The earlier footnote in Martin Rispens was dicta. The holding applies to a consumer against a manufacturer.
Goodin read Alternative A as speaking only to horizontal privity.
Goodin reached economic loss.
The claim that survived in Goodin was the implied warranty.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Goodin holding

q: A corporate buyer of a $2 million printing press sues the remote manufacturer in Indiana for lost profits on implied merchantability, citing Goodin. What is the best response?
o: Goodin's holding is limited to a consumer against a manufacturer.
Goodin abolished privity for every buyer in every state.
Goodin bars lost-profit claims by all buyers.
Goodin requires an express warranty.
oe: Correct. Those are the case's limits. Commercial buyers can bargain and rarely fit its rationale.
It's Indiana law, limited to its context, and courts are divided.
It doesn't state that rule.
The holding was on the implied warranty.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Limits of Goodin

q: A consumer revokes against a remote manufacturer. The dealer's price was $40,000, and the manufacturer got $33,000 from the dealer. Which statement fits the text?
o: Whether she can get a refund, and of which price, is open.
The refund is always $33,000, the maker's price.
The refund is always $40,000, the consumer's price.
A statute bars revocation against remote sellers.
oe: Correct. See pp. 338-339. The difference in price is exactly why the question is hard.
The text doesn't settle that.
The text doesn't settle that either.
The statute doesn't address it.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Refund from remote seller

q: A third-party vendor sells a defective hoverboard on Amazon, and Amazon stores and ships it. The buyer argues Amazon is a seller by entrustment under § 2-403(2). Which is NOT a reason given that the argument fails?
o: Amazon is exempt from the UCC as a federal carrier.
Amazon may never possess the goods, and the vendor's identity is disclosed.
An entrustee is not necessarily "the seller."
Amazon's terms disclaim implied warranties anyway.
oe: Correct. That's not a reason. The reasons: Amazon may never possess the goods and the vendor's identity is disclosed; an entrustee isn't necessarily "the seller"; and Amazon's terms disclaim implied warranties.
A given reason.
A given reason.
A given reason.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Amazon

q: Manufacturer warrants a copier "3 years from purchase" and sells it to Distributor on June 1, 2021. Distributor disclaims all warranties and sells to Retailer on Dec. 1, 2021. Retailer warrants it for 1 year and sells to Buyer on April 1, 2022. In a privity-abolished state, the copier fails on Nov. 1, 2022. Who is exposed?
o: Retailer and likely Manufacturer, but not Distributor.
All three, since privity is abolished.
Only Retailer, since Buyer dealt only with Retailer.
Only Manufacturer, as the source of the defect.
oe: Correct. Whether a warranty on forms Buyer never saw reaches Buyer is a real issue, but the Manufacturer's period hasn't run on either reading.
Distributor's disclaimer is effective.
Privity is abolished here.
Retailer's warranty is still running.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Copier chain: Nov. 2022

q: Same chain, but the copier fails on Nov. 1, 2024. When does Manufacturer's "3 years from purchase" warranty cover it?
o: Only if "purchase" means Buyer's purchase.
In all cases, since it runs from the last sale.
Never, since it ran from the sale to Retailer.
Only if Retailer's warranty is still running.
oe: Correct. The ambiguity decides the case. Implied warranties remain only if the defect existed at tender and the suit is timely under § 2-725.
The wording is ambiguous.
Manufacturer sold to Distributor, and the language is open.
The two are independent.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Copier chain: Nov. 2024
pre: Manufacturer warrants a copier "3 years from purchase" and sells it to Distributor on June 1, 2021. Distributor disclaims all warranties and sells to Retailer on Dec. 1, 2021. Retailer warrants it for 1 year and sells to Buyer on April 1, 2022. In a privity-abolished state, the copier fails on Nov. 1, 2022. Who is exposed?

q: Same chain, but privity isn't abolished. Buyer sues Retailer on the implied warranty and wins. Why can't Retailer pass the loss up the chain?
o: Distributor's disclaimer cuts off Retailer's recourse.
Retailer isn't a merchant in copiers.
The limitations period has run against everyone.
A retailer can never have recourse up the chain.
oe: Correct. The implied claim runs only against Retailer. Manufacturer's express warranty may survive, though it wasn't a public statement.
It is, which is why it gave the warranty.
Nothing on the facts says so.
It can, absent a disclaimer.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Privity kept: recourse gap
pre: Manufacturer warrants a copier "3 years from purchase" and sells it to Distributor on June 1, 2021. Distributor disclaims all warranties and sells to Retailer on Dec. 1, 2021. Retailer warrants it for 1 year and sells to Buyer on April 1, 2022. In a privity-abolished state, the copier fails on Nov. 1, 2022. Who is exposed?

q: Same chain; Buyer is a corporation. Its vice president takes the copier home, where it starts a fire destroying his house. No one is hurt. Which alternative gives him a claim against Retailer?
o: Only Alternative C, if "injured" includes property.
Alternative A, because he's an officer of the buyer.
Alternative B, because he's a natural person.
All three alternatives.
oe: Correct. VP isn't the buyer, so this is horizontal. Alt. A needs family, household or guest, and injury in person. Alt. B needs injury in person. Tort remains.
Alt. A concerns family, household and home guests.
Alt. B requires injury in person.
Only C could cover a property-only loss.
topic: Wk 10 · XXIII · Privity & remote sellers (§ 2-318) — Fire at VP's home
pre: Manufacturer warrants a copier "3 years from purchase" and sells it to Distributor on June 1, 2021. Distributor disclaims all warranties and sells to Retailer on Dec. 1, 2021. Retailer warrants it for 1 year and sells to Buyer on April 1, 2022. In a privity-abolished state, the copier fails on Nov. 1, 2022. Who is exposed?

q: Under a contract calling for payment before shipment, Alder Mills refuses to ship because Beck has not paid. Beck sues for nondelivery. Separately, a fire without fault destroys Alder's identified goods before risk passes. What should be asked first in each dispute?
o: Whether the refusal was justified, a breach, or neither.
Which remedy gives Alder the highest recovery.
Whether Beck has already covered elsewhere.
Whether Alder can show it is a lost-volume seller.
oe: Correct. Walk the facts: was the refusal justified (buyer failed to pay first or to answer a proper demand), or a breach, or is neither party in breach, as with casualty to the goods? Then ask about excuse and limits.
The remedy comes only after breach is settled.
Cover presupposes a seller's breach.
That's a damages detail far down the road.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Justified refusal to deliver

q: Carver sold Lund a bandsaw, accepted in March. Lund hasn't paid by December and argues that "commercially reasonable time" has passed, so Carver can't sue for the price. Is Lund right?
o: No, because that phrase limits only lost or damaged goods.
Yes, because a price action must be brought within that time.
Yes, unless Carver gives notice of a resale.
No, but Carver may recover only market damages.
oe: Correct. Section 2-709(1)(a); see p. 399 n.1.
The limit doesn't apply to accepted goods; § 2-725 governs timing.
Resale notice has nothing to do with accepted goods.
The price is available.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Action for the price: accepted

q: A buyer accepts a $6,400 custom sign in the wrong color, spends $1,300 reprinting brochures to match, and pays nothing. Assume the $1,300 is recoverable under § 2-715, and the value difference is $500. What is the seller's net recovery if the buyer gave proper notice?
o: $4,600: the price less $500 and $1,300.
$6,400: acceptance bars any offset.
$5,900: only the value difference may be deducted.
Zero: a nonconforming sign can't support the price.
oe: Correct. The worked example at p. 400.
Acceptance doesn't bar damages (§§ 2-714, 2-717).
Recoverable consequential damages may also be deducted.
Accepted goods support the price.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Custom sign offset

q: Invoices from Reed Supply say: "Title to all goods remains with Seller until paid in full." A buyer takes delivery and doesn't pay. Reed claims it still owns the goods and sends a truck to retrieve them from the buyer's locked warehouse. What is the effect of the clause?
o: Title passes on delivery; Reed has only a security interest.
Reed remains the owner and may retrieve its goods by any means.
The clause is void as a penalty.
The clause turns the transaction into a lease.
oe: Correct. Sections 1-201(b)(35), 2-401(1), 9-109(a)(5). Reed is a secured party at most, and must proceed under § 9-609 without breach of the peace.
The reservation is limited to a security interest (§ 2-401(1)).
It isn't void; it's recharacterized.
It's a sale with a retained security interest.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Title retention clause

q: Under a cash sale, Fenn hands over a check at delivery of a tractor. The check bounces five days later. Fenn won't return the tractor. Which is correct?
o: It may reclaim under § 2-507 within a reasonable time.
It has only a claim for the price, since title passed.
It must first prove that Fenn is insolvent.
It must demand the tractor within 10 days after receipt.
oe: Correct. Payment due on delivery plus a failed payment device. A check at delivery counts (§ 2-511 cmts. 4-6). A credit sale or post-dated check doesn't.
Section 2-507 adds reclamation for failed payment.
That's § 2-702; § 2-507 doesn't need insolvency.
That's § 2-702(2); § 2-507 uses a reasonable time.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Bounced check reclamation

q: On April 1, Moss sells tile on 30-day credit to a contractor, who received the tile on April 3 while insolvent. Moss discovers this on April 20 and demands the tile that day. The contractor never misrepresented anything. Can Moss reclaim?
o: No, because the demand came more than 10 days after receipt.
Yes, because the 10 days run from discovery of insolvency.
Yes, because a credit sale may be reclaimed for 3 months.
No, because reclamation is unavailable for credit sales.
oe: Correct. The clock runs from receipt, not discovery.
They run from receipt.
Three months belongs only to the misrepresentation exception.
Section 2-702(2) exists for credit sales.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — § 2-702(2) timing

q: Under § 2-702(2), Sand reclaims the insolvent buyer's goods, and they have fallen in value by $4,000. Sand also incurred $300 trucking them back. Can Sand sue for either sum?
o: No, because reclaiming excludes all other remedies for those goods.
Yes, both, as ordinary § 2-706 damages.
Only the $300, as incidental damages.
Only the $4,000, as market damages.
oe: Correct. Section 2-702(3). Possibly reclamation rests on rescission for fraud, and other creditors shouldn't be pushed further behind.
Section 2-702(3) bars them.
Apparently even incidentals are excluded.
Section 2-702(3) bars that too.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Reclamation excludes other remedies

q: An insolvent buyer receives goods on credit on May 1 and on May 5 sells them to a buyer in ordinary course. The seller demands them from the second buyer on May 8. Who wins?
o: The second buyer, because reclamation is subject to its rights.
The seller, because it acted within the 10 days.
The seller, because the first buyer's title was void.
Neither, because the goods go to a bankruptcy trustee.
oe: Correct. Section 2-702(3).
Timeliness doesn't defeat a buyer in ordinary course.
Voidable title can pass good title.
No bankruptcy is on the facts.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Reclamation vs. purchasers

q: Supplier delivers 4,000 gallons of milk on credit to an insolvent dairy, which puts it into a vat with 5,000 other gallons and turns half the vat into ice cream. Within 10 days, Supplier demands the milk back. Which result fits the statute?
o: About 2,000 gallons, and none of the ice cream.
All 4,000 gallons out of what remains.
Nothing, because commingling ends the right.
Its share of the milk and of the ice cream.
oe: Correct. Treat the milk as fungible (§ 2-105(4)). The ice cream is no longer the goods sold. This is worked from the statute; the casebook cites Wheeling-Pittsburgh and Charter.
Its share of the commingled mass is limited to 4/9.
A share of a fungible bulk can be identified (§ 2-105(4)).
The ice cream isn't the goods sold.
topic: Wk 11 · XXIV · Seller's remedies: price & reclamation (§§ 2-703, 2-709, 2-507, 2-702) — Milk in the vat

q: Under a contract for 12 shipments on 30-day credit, seller Oak Co. discovers that buyer Finch is insolvent after four shipments, two of them still unpaid but not yet due. What may Oak require before making the fifth shipment?
o: Cash for the fifth shipment and for all goods already delivered.
Cash for the fifth shipment only.
Nothing, because the 30-day credit term still governs.
Return of all four earlier shipments.
oe: Correct. Section 2-702(1). Oak may refuse delivery except for cash, including payment for goods previously delivered.
Section 2-702(1) includes all goods previously delivered.
Insolvency overrides the credit term.
Reclamation has its own limits under § 2-702(2).
topic: Wk 11 · XXV · Withholding, stopping in transit & cancelling (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705) — Insolvent buyer, cash only

q: Seattle Gems ships diamonds under a negotiable bill naming itself consignee, then tells the carrier, Federated, to stop. The bill is still with Seattle's agent, and it isn't surrendered. Must Federated obey now?
o: No, not until the bill is surrendered.
Yes, immediately, because the seller is the consignee.
No, because a carrier need only obey the buyer.
Yes, but only if the seller posts a bond.
oe: Correct. Section 2-705(3)(c). Federated should hold and ask for the bill.
Section 2-705(3)(c) lets the carrier wait for the bill.
The holder of the document controls, and that isn't the buyer.
No bond is mentioned in the statute.
topic: Wk 11 · XXV · Withholding, stopping in transit & cancelling (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705) — Negotiable bill

q: A buyer fails to make a required down payment on a single-delivery contract, and the seller wants to cancel. Which is correct?
o: It may cancel on any buyer breach, keeping its damages.
It may cancel only after a 30-day cure period.
It may cancel only for a material breach.
It may cancel, but that waives its damages.
oe: Correct. Sections 2-703(f), 2-106(4).
There's no such period.
In a non-installment contract, any breach will do.
Cancellation doesn't waive them (§ 2-106(4)).
topic: Wk 11 · XXV · Withholding, stopping in transit & cancelling (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705) — Cancel a single contract

q: Seattle Gems ships a parcel of diamonds F.O.B. seller. The buyer misses a funds transfer and has defaulted to its main lender. Seattle wants to stop delivery. What is the key issue?
o: Nonpayment alone won't do; is the buyer actually insolvent?
Any failure to pay allows stopping any shipment.
A default to a lender is conclusive proof of insolvency.
The F.O.B. seller term means the seller can't stop.
oe: Correct. Ask whether the buyer has generally ceased paying debts or can't pay as they come due. Holding the bill in its own name also gives Seattle practical control (§ 2-505).
The size limit applies to a parcel.
It's only evidence.
The shipping term doesn't remove § 2-705.
topic: Wk 11 · XXV · Withholding, stopping in transit & cancelling (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705) — Diamonds in a parcel

q: A distributor bought 500 stoves in two lots. It accepted the first 250, and its $20,000 check (20% due on delivery) bounced. The other 250 sit in the seller's warehouse. Which is the best first advice?
o: Withhold, sue on the check, and demand assurance before cancelling.
Cancel the whole contract at once for any breach.
Repossess the first 250 stoves immediately.
Ship the second lot, then sue for both prices.
oe: Correct. A bounced check leaves the debt alive. Failure to give assurance within 30 days is repudiation, which supports cancelling and reselling. Section 2-507 reclamation is doubtful: only 20% was due on delivery.
This is an installment contract, so substantial impairment is needed.
There's no security interest, and reclamation is limited.
The seller needn't keep shipping (§ 2-703(a)).
topic: Wk 11 · XXV · Withholding, stopping in transit & cancelling (§§ 2-702, 2-703, 2-705) — Stoves: bounced check

q: A gallery contracts to sell a $10,000 lithograph, one of a kind. The buyer defaults. The print is worth $9,000. The gallery resells it for $9,000. What are its damages (no incidentals)?
o: $1,000 under § 2-706, or the same under § 2-708(1).
$10,000: the full price, since it's unique.
$9,000: the amount of the resale.
Nothing: the gallery found another buyer.
oe: Correct. Worked example, pp. 408-410.
The goods sold, so no price action lies.
The gallery keeps that.
It still lost $1,000.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Lithograph: lower value

q: Same contract, but the gallery holds unlimited prints of a $10,000 lithograph and would have made both sales. Its print costs $4,000. The second sale at $10,000 happens anyway. What is the proper measure?
o: $6,000 lost profit, because the resale isn't a substitute.
Zero, because it resold at the contract price.
$10,000, the full contract price.
$4,000, its cost of the print.
oe: Correct. The dealer would have made both sales, so the breach cost it one sale.
The resale isn't a true substitute.
It still has its goods, and can resell.
Cost isn't the measure.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Lithograph: unlimited supply
pre: A gallery contracts to sell a $10,000 lithograph, one of a kind. The buyer defaults. The print is worth $9,000. The gallery resells it for $9,000. What are its damages (no incidentals)?

q: After a buyer breached a $50,000 contract, Crane Co. privately resold the goods for $42,000 in a commercially reasonable manner, without telling the buyer. Crane sues for $8,000 under § 2-706. What happens?
o: The § 2-706 claim fails, but Crane may use § 2-708(1).
Crane wins, because notice is required only for auctions.
Crane loses all damages for failing to give notice.
Crane must recover the price under § 2-709 instead.
oe: Correct. Section 2-706(3). A bad resale only loses this measure (cmt. 2).
Private sales need notice of intent to resell.
It falls back on § 2-708.
The goods have been resold.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Private sale notice

q: A seller botches a resale by failing to give notice. The purchaser buys in good faith. The original buyer sues the purchaser for the goods, and also demands the $3,000 by which the resale exceeded the contract price. What happens?
o: The purchaser takes free, and the seller keeps the $3,000.
The purchaser loses, because the resale was defective.
The seller must pay the $3,000 profit to the buyer.
Both the resale and the original contract are void.
oe: Correct. Sections 2-706(5)-(6). A person in the position of a seller or a buyer who rightfully rejected must account in some cases, but a seller keeps the profit.
A good-faith purchaser takes free anyway (§ 2-706(5)).
Section 2-706(6) says no accounting.
Neither is void.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Resale to good faith purchaser

q: After a buyer's breach, a cranberry seller points to several later sales as the "resale." They were of a different product, on special contracts, and in much smaller loads. In another case an oil seller's resale came six weeks after breach, when it had sold conforming oil the very next day. How would the cited cases treat these?
o: Neither qualifies under those cases.
Both qualify, since a seller may pick any later sale.
Only the cranberry sales qualify.
Only the oil resale qualifies, since oil is fungible.
oe: Correct. Note the parallel to a buyer showing which purchases were cover.
The sale must be a true substitute.
Wisconsin Cranberry rejected them.
Apex Oil rejected the resale for delay.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Sales not substitutes

q: A maker has half-built a custom machine when the buyer repudiates. Finishing costs $40,000, the finished machine would sell for $90,000 to another customer, and scrap value is $10,000. What may it do?
o: Finish and resell, if that's sound commercial judgment.
It must stop work at once and sell for scrap.
It must finish, whatever the cost and whatever the market.
It must get the court's permission first.
oe: Correct. Section 2-704(2). It may complete or cease and scrap, or proceed in another reasonable manner.
Not if finishing better avoids loss.
Only if commercially reasonable.
No permission is needed.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Unfinished goods

q: A seller's contract is at $100 per unit. The buyer repudiates. The seller resells at $92, while market price at the time and place for tender is $80. It claims $20 per unit under § 2-708(1). Under Peace River, what is the result, and what is the counterargument?
o: It may claim $20 despite the resale, though § 1-305 argues for $8.
It's limited to $8, as a resale always locks in the seller.
It recovers $28, adding both measures.
It gets nothing because it mitigated by reselling.
oe: Correct. Peace River: a fixed-price contract allocates market risk, resale isn't required, and the UCC rejects election of remedies.
Peace River rejects that.
Resale and market can't be stacked.
Mitigating doesn't erase the claim.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Peace River

q: A manufacturer claims lost-volume status under § 2-708(2), proving it had the plant capacity to make the breached units as well as what it actually sold. What must it also show under R.E. Davis v. Diasonics?
o: That making the extra units would have been profitable.
That it advertised for replacement buyers.
That the market price of the goods fell.
That it would have resold to the same customer.
oe: Correct. Capacity alone isn't enough. Under diminishing returns, the next sale may stop being worthwhile, so presumed lost profit would overcompensate.
Advertising isn't an element; Diasonics asks about capacity and profitability.
A falling market goes to § 2-708(1), not to lost-volume status.
The question is whether the seller would have made both sales, not who bought.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Diasonics

q: A lost-volume seller's contract price was $100,000. Its variable costs for this order would have been $60,000, none of which it spent, and it would have allocated $15,000 of overhead to the order. Separately, before the breach it spent $4,000 on job-specific tooling it can't reuse. Ignoring incidentals, what does § 2-708(2) yield?
o: $44,000: price minus variable costs plus reliance.
$25,000: profit after overhead.
$40,000: reliance isn't added.
$100,000: the contract price.
oe: Correct. Overhead is added back, so recovery is sale price minus variable costs ($40,000) plus unreimbursed reliance ($4,000).
The statute adds overhead back.
"Due allowance for costs reasonably incurred" adds it.
It avoided the variable costs, so profit is the measure.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Lost-profit math

q: A buyer breaches a contract to buy metal at $5. Market at tender is $3. The seller's own profit would have been only $0.25. The buyer argues damages can't exceed $0.25 a unit. What does Trans World Metals support?
o: It gets $2 a unit, because lost profit isn't a ceiling.
It gets $0.25, since § 1-305 always caps it at profit.
It gets nothing, since it must have hedged.
It gets both $2 and $0.25.
oe: Correct. Section 2-708(2) applies only when other measures are inadequate, not when they are higher.
The leading case rejects that.
Hedging isn't on the facts.
The measures can't be stacked.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — No ceiling

q: A lathe seller contracted to sell for $90,000. Cost of the lathe $80,000, $2,000 of parts, $1,500 of preparation, and $500 overhead. After breach it pays a $1,000 cancellation fee and can reuse only $800 of the parts. It's a lost-volume seller. What is the recovery?
o: $8,700: $6,500 profit plus $2,200 reliance.
$6,000: profit after overhead.
$6,500: reliance isn't added.
$9,500: reliance includes all $2,000 of parts.
oe: Correct. $90,000 minus $83,500 = $6,500 (overhead isn't deducted). Add $1,000 cancellation and $1,200 of parts it can't reuse.
Overhead isn't deducted.
Unreimbursed reliance is added.
The $800 it can reuse must be credited.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Lathe lost profit

q: A seller made spring-season fabric for a buyer. After breach it made little resale effort for months, in a market down 50%, and sold part in the next season at a low price. Which is correct under Foxco?
o: It may recover the price: reasonable effort is enough.
It loses, because the goods still had some value.
It loses, because it needed to try all year.
It loses, because it had to hold a public auction first.
oe: Correct. The goods need not be worthless.
The goods needn't be worthless.
Reasonable efforts are enough.
No auction is required.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Foxco

q: A buyer repudiates a contract for 100,000 gallons at $5 F.O.B. Miami; the seller would have paid 10¢/gal freight. The seller properly resells at $4.75 F.O.B. Cincinnati, paying $1,000 in storage. What are damages?
o: $26,000: saved freight isn't deducted.
$25,000: incidentals and savings are ignored.
$36,000: saved freight is added.

Expenses saved are deducted.
Both count.
It's deducted.
topic: Wk 11 · XXVI · Seller's damages: resale, market, lost profit, price (§§ 2-704, 2-706, 2-708 to 2-710) — Fuel resale math

q: A seller has spent $4,000 on a $6,400 custom sign, with $800 to finish it. The buyer repudiates. Salvage nets $100. Or $2,000 of modification gives a 50% chance of a $5,000 sale. Which is the sound analysis?
o: Salvage is safe, modifying is defensible, and finishing makes no sense.
It must finish the sign, since that's the contract.
It must modify, because the expected value is positive.
It must abandon the sign without any salvage.
oe: Correct. Salvage recovery from buyer is $5,500. Modify: 50% × $5,000 minus $2,000 = $500. If a court finds it unreasonable, the seller eats the $2,000.
Nobody else wants a finished sign.
